en-A1-0.b:
English has 26 letters but about 44 sounds, so spelling and pronunciation often differ.

  • Letter names: A [eɪ], E [iː], I [aɪ], O [əʊ], U [juː]. Careful: E sounds like French « i », I like « aïe ».
  • th: tongue between the teeth: think [θ], this [ð]. Not « s » or « z ».
  • h is pronounced: house, hello (except hour, honest).
  • Short vs long vowels: ship / sheep, full / fool.
  • Silent letters: know, write, listen, island.
  • Word stress: one syllable is stronger: PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy.
  • -ed: [t] worked, [d] played, [ɪd] wanted.

Common mistake: dropping the h (« I 'ave ») or saying « zis » for this.
en-A1-0.t:
L'anglais a 26 lettres mais environ 44 sons : l'orthographe et la prononciation diffèrent souvent.

  • Nom des lettres : A [eɪ], E [iː], I [aɪ], O [əʊ], U [juː]. Attention : le E se dit comme le « i » français, le I comme « aïe ».
  • th : la langue entre les dents : think [θ], this [ð]. Ni « s » ni « z ».
  • Le h se prononce (aspiré) : house, hello (sauf hour, honest).
  • Voyelles courtes / longues : ship / sheep, full / fool.
  • Lettres muettes : know, write, listen, island.
  • Accent tonique : une syllabe est plus forte : PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy.
  • -ed : [t] worked, [d] played, [ɪd] wanted.

Erreur fréquente : ne pas prononcer le h (« I 'ave ») ou dire « zis » pour this.
e: I think this is the right house.
She has a ship, not a sheep.
We wanted to watch a film.
q: Which word has a long vowel?

en-A1-3.b:
Subject pronouns do the action; object pronouns receive it.

subjectobject
Ime
youyou
hehim
sheher
itit
weus
theythem
  • She loves him. He loves her.
  • After a preposition: object: with me, for them, to us.
  • it for things and animals; they for plural (people and things).
  • you = singular and plural, informal and formal (no « vous » form).

Common mistake: « Me and him went » → He and I went; « between you and I » → between you and me.
en-A1-3.t:
Les pronoms sujets font l'action ; les pronoms compléments la reçoivent.

sujetcomplément
I (je)me (me, moi)
you (tu/vous)you
he (il)him (le, lui)
she (elle)her (la, lui)
it (il/elle, chose)it
we (nous)us (nous)
they (ils/elles)them (les, leur)
  • She loves him. He loves her.
  • Après une préposition : complément : with me, for them, to us.
  • it pour les choses et les animaux ; they pour le pluriel (personnes et choses).
  • you = singulier et pluriel, familier et poli (pas de forme « vous » distincte).

Erreur fréquente : « Me and him went » → He and I went ; « between you and I » → between you and me.

en-A1-5.b:
In the present simple, use do / does for questions and negatives.

  • Question: Do + I/you/we/they + verb: Do you speak Dutch? · Does + he/she/it + verb: Does she work here?
  • Negative: don't (do not) / doesn't (does not) + verb: I don't eat meat. He doesn't drive.
  • After does/doesn't, the verb has no -s: Does he live…? He doesn't live…
  • Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.
  • With question words: Where do you live? What does he do?

Exception: be and can don't use do: Are you tired? I can't swim.

Common mistake: « Does she lives? » → Does she live?; « You speak English? » (in writing) → Do you speak English?
en-A1-5.t:
Au présent simple, on utilise do / does pour les questions et la négation.

  • Question : Do + I/you/we/they + verbe : Do you speak Dutch? · Does + he/she/it + verbe : Does she work here?
  • Négation : don't (do not) / doesn't (does not) + verbe : I don't eat meat. He doesn't drive.
  • Après does/doesn't, le verbe ne prend pas de -s : Does he live…? He doesn't live…
  • Réponses courtes : Yes, I do. / No, she doesn't.
  • Avec un mot interrogatif : Where do you live? What does he do?

Exception : be et can n'utilisent pas do : Are you tired? I can't swim.

Erreur fréquente : « Does she lives? » → Does she live? ; « You speak English? » (à l'écrit) → Do you speak English?
e: What do you do for a living?
q: Short answer: Do you smoke? — No, I ___

en-A1-6.b:
Most nouns add -s in the plural: book → books, car → cars.

  • -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -z → -es: bus → buses, dish → dishes, box → boxes.
  • Consonant + y → -ies: city → cities, baby → babies (but vowel + y: day → days).
  • -f / -fe → -ves: knife → knives, wife → wives, half → halves.
  • Some -o → -oes: potato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes (but photos, pianos).

Irregular: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice. Same form: sheep, fish.

Pronunciation of -s: [s] books, [z] cars, [ɪz] buses.

Common mistake: « childs, peoples, informations » → children, people, information (uncountable).
en-A1-6.t:
La plupart des noms prennent -s au pluriel : book → books, car → cars.

  • -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -z → -es : bus → buses, dish → dishes, box → boxes.
  • Consonne + y → -ies : city → cities, baby → babies (mais voyelle + y : day → days).
  • -f / -fe → -ves : knife → knives, wife → wives, half → halves.
  • Certains -o → -oes : potato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes (mais photos, pianos).

Irréguliers : man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice. Forme identique : sheep, fish.

Prononciation du -s : [s] books, [z] cars, [ɪz] buses.

Erreur fréquente : « childs, peoples, informations » → children, people, information (indénombrable).
e: Ghent and Bruges are beautiful cities.

en-A1-7.b:
Possessive adjectives go before a noun:

I → mywe → our
you → youryou → your
he → his, she → her, it → itsthey → their
  • his = belongs to a man, her = belongs to a woman (the owner decides, not the object!): Marie and her father. Paul and his mother.
  • its (no apostrophe) for things/animals: The dog wags its tail. (it's = it is)

's for people: John's car, my sister's house. Plural in -s: s': my parents' house. Irregular plural: the children's toys.

Common mistake: « Marie and his father » → Marie and her father; « the car of John » → John's car.
en-A1-7.t:
Les adjectifs possessifs se placent devant un nom :

I → my (mon/ma/mes)we → our (notre/nos)
you → your (ton/ta/tes)you → your (votre/vos)
he → his, she → her, it → its (son/sa/ses)they → their (leur/leurs)
  • his = appartient à un homme, her = à une femme (c'est le possesseur qui décide, pas l'objet !) : Marie and her father. Paul and his mother.
  • its (sans apostrophe) pour les choses/animaux : The dog wags its tail. (it's = it is)

's pour les personnes : John's car (la voiture de John), my sister's house. Pluriel en -s : s' : my parents' house. Pluriel irrégulier : the children's toys.

Erreur fréquente : « Marie and his father » → Marie and her father ; « the car of John » → John's car.
e: Paul is talking to his mother.

en-A1-8.b:
Demonstratives show distance and number:

near (here)far (there)
singularthis bookthat book
pluralthese booksthose books
  • No masculine/feminine: this man, this woman.
  • Alone (as pronouns): This is my friend. Are those yours?
  • On the phone: Hello, this is Collins.
  • that also refers to something just said: That's a good idea!

Pronunciation: this [ðɪs] (short i), these [ðiːz] (long ee).

Common mistake: « this books » → these books; « these book » → this book.
en-A1-8.t:
Les démonstratifs indiquent la distance et le nombre :

près (ici)loin (là-bas)
singulierthis book (ce livre-ci)that book (ce livre-là)
plurielthese booksthose books
  • Pas de masculin/féminin : this man, this woman.
  • Seuls (pronoms) : This is my friend. Are those yours?
  • Au téléphone : Hello, this is Collins. (C'est Collins)
  • that renvoie aussi à ce qui vient d'être dit : That's a good idea!

Prononciation : this [ðɪs] (i court), these [ðiːz] (ee long).

Erreur fréquente : « this books » → these books ; « these book » → this book.
e: Look at that house over there.
q: On the phone: Hello, ___ is Anna.
"___'s a good idea!" (what you just said)
___ woman over there is my boss.

en-A1-9.b:
There is / there are = il y a.

  • There is (there's) + singular or uncountable: There's a bank near here. There is some milk.
  • There are + plural: There are three bedrooms.
  • Question: Is there a pharmacy? Are there any shops?
  • Negative: There isn't a lift. There aren't any chairs.
  • Past: There was a problem. There were many people.

Don't confuse: there (place), their (possessive), they're (they are).

Common mistake: « It has a bank near here » (from French « il y a ») → There is a bank near here; « There is many people » → There are many people.
en-A1-9.t:
There is / there are = il y a.

  • There is (there's) + singulier ou indénombrable : There's a bank near here. There is some milk.
  • There are + pluriel : There are three bedrooms.
  • Question : Is there a pharmacy? Are there any shops?
  • Négation : There isn't a lift. There aren't any chairs.
  • Passé : There was a problem. There were many people.

Ne pas confondre : there (lieu), their (possessif), they're (they are).

Erreur fréquente : « It has a bank near here » (calque de « il y a ») → There is a bank near here ; « There is many people » → There are many people.
e: There's a supermarket on the corner.
There are two bathrooms in the flat.
Is there a train to Brussels tonight?
There were a lot of people at the party.

en-A1-10.b:
can expresses ability, possibility and permission. It is the same for all persons (no -s) and is followed by the base verb (no to).

  • Ability: I can swim. She can speak three languages.
  • Permission / request: Can I open the window? Can you help me?
  • Negative: can't (cannot): I can't come tonight.
  • Question: Can you drive? — Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
  • Past: could / couldn't: I couldn't sleep.
  • More polite: Could you repeat that, please?

Pronunciation: can is often weak [kən]; can't is strong [kɑːnt] (UK).

Common mistake: « She cans swim », « I can to swim » → She can swim.
en-A1-10.t:
can exprime la capacité, la possibilité et la permission. Il est identique à toutes les personnes (pas de -s) et suivi du verbe de base (sans to).

  • Capacité : I can swim. She can speak three languages.
  • Permission / demande : Can I open the window? Can you help me?
  • Négation : can't (cannot) : I can't come tonight.
  • Question : Can you drive? — Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
  • Passé : could / couldn't : I couldn't sleep.
  • Plus poli : Could you repeat that, please?

Prononciation : can est souvent faible [kən] ; can't est fort [kɑːnt] (UK).

Erreur fréquente : « She cans swim », « I can to swim » → She can swim.
e: I can speak English and French.
Can you help me with this?
She can't come to the meeting.
Could you speak more slowly, please?
When I was young, I could run fast.

en-A1-11.b:
Prepositions of time:

  • at + clock time / night / weekend (UK): at 8 o'clock, at night, at the weekend
  • on + day / date: on Monday, on 5 May, on my birthday
  • in + month / year / season / part of day: in June, in 2025, in winter, in the morning

Prepositions of place:

  • at + a point / address / event: at the station, at home, at work, at 12 Main Street
  • on + surface / street / floor: on the table, on the wall, on Main Street, on the 2nd floor
  • in + inside / city / country: in the box, in Ghent, in Belgium
  • Others: under, next to, between, behind, in front of, opposite, near

Movement: to: I go to work. (but go home, no to)

Common mistake: « in Monday » → on Monday; « I go to home » → I go home.
en-A1-11.t:
Prépositions de temps :

  • at + heure / la nuit / le week-end (UK) : at 8 o'clock, at night, at the weekend
  • on + jour / date : on Monday, on 5 May, on my birthday
  • in + mois / année / saison / partie de la journée : in June, in 2025, in winter, in the morning

Prépositions de lieu :

  • at + un point / une adresse / un événement : at the station, at home, at work, at 12 Main Street
  • on + surface / rue / étage : on the table, on the wall, on Main Street, on the 2nd floor
  • in + à l'intérieur / ville / pays : in the box, in Ghent, in Belgium
  • Autres : under (sous), next to (à côté de), between, behind (derrière), in front of (devant), opposite (en face), near (près)

Mouvement : to : I go to work. (mais go home, sans to)

Erreur fréquente : « in Monday » → on Monday ; « I go to home » → I go home.
e: The meeting is at 9 o'clock on Monday.
Your keys are on the table.

en-A1-12.b:
Countable nouns can be counted (an apple, two apples). Uncountable nouns cannot (water, money, bread, information, advice, furniture, news) — no a/an, no plural.

  • some: positive sentences (and offers/requests): I have some friends. I need some water. Would you like some tea?
  • any: questions and negatives: Do you have any money? I don't have any brothers.
  • How many + countable: How many children? · How much + uncountable: How much time?
  • a lot of for both: a lot of people, a lot of work.

To count uncountables: a piece of advice, a glass of water, a loaf of bread.

Common mistake: « an information, advices, furnitures » → some information, some advice, furniture.
en-A1-12.t:
Les noms dénombrables se comptent (an apple, two apples). Les indénombrables non (water, money, bread, information, advice, furniture, news) — pas de a/an, pas de pluriel.

  • some : phrases affirmatives (et offres/demandes) : I have some friends. I need some water. Would you like some tea?
  • any : questions et négations : Do you have any money? I don't have any brothers.
  • How many + dénombrable : How many children? · How much + indénombrable : How much time?
  • a lot of pour les deux : a lot of people, a lot of work.

Pour compter un indénombrable : a piece of advice (un conseil), a glass of water, a loaf of bread.

Erreur fréquente : « an information, advices, furnitures » → some information, some advice, furniture (contrairement au français « des informations, des conseils, des meubles »).
e: Can I have some water, please?
She gave me some good advice.
q: She gave me two pieces of ___

en-A1-13.b:
The imperative gives orders, instructions and advice. Use the base verb, without a subject:

  • Open the door. Sit down. Turn left.
  • Negative: Don't + verb: Don't touch that! Don't be late.
  • With let's (= let us) for suggestions: Let's go! Let's not wait.
  • More polite: add please, or use a question: Please sit down. Could you close the door?
  • Friendly emphasis: Do come in! Have a nice day!

The same form is used for one person or several (no « vous » form).

Common mistake: « No touch! » → Don't touch!; « You sit down » sounds rude → Sit down, please.
en-A1-13.t:
L'impératif sert à donner des ordres, des instructions et des conseils. On utilise le verbe de base, sans sujet :

  • Open the door. Sit down. Turn left.
  • Négation : Don't + verbe : Don't touch that! Don't be late.
  • Avec let's (= let us) pour proposer : Let's go! (Allons-y !) Let's not wait.
  • Plus poli : ajoute please, ou pose une question : Please sit down. Could you close the door?
  • Insistance amicale : Do come in! Have a nice day!

La même forme s'utilise pour une ou plusieurs personnes (pas de forme « vous »).

Erreur fréquente : « No touch! » → Don't touch! ; « You sit down » paraît impoli → Sit down, please.
e: Turn right at the traffic lights.
